title: Neuromyelitis optica: a challenging diagnosis at secondary hospital
case_prompt:
An 18-year-old African‐descent woman with no prior medical history presented with 3 months of 14‐kg weight loss, daily headache, and intermittent vomiting. Two weeks after symptom onset, she developed binocular diplopia and a burning sensation in her lower limbs that progressed over 1 month to involve the face and scalp, accompanied by gait instability. A few days before admission, she noted worsening lower‐limb weakness that ascended to the upper limbs, new trunk sensory changes, and urinary incontinence.

On examination, she appeared emaciated and pale but hemodynamically stable. Cognitive function was intact. Neurologic examination revealed asymmetric tetraparesis: right lower limb strength 0/5, right upper limb 3/5; left lower limb 1/5, left upper limb 3/5. Deep‐tendon reflexes were absent in the upper limbs and brisk with extensor plantar responses in the lower limbs. Sensation was impaired in all modalities below a T2 sensory level. Cranial‐nerve examination was normal. A urinary catheter was placed for bladder dysfunction.

Laboratory studies showed negative results for antinuclear antibodies, hepatitis B and C serologies, HIV, HTLV, and syphilis. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. Lumbar cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis demonstrated 11 white cells/mm3 (93% lymphocytes), elevated protein of 63 mg/dL, normal glucose, an adenosine deaminase level of 1.23 U/L, and lactate of 17.6 mg/dL; India ink preparation and aerobic, fungal, and acid‐fast bacillus cultures were negative. Noncontrast CT scans of the brain and spine were unremarkable.

Three days after admission, she developed complete paralysis of all four limbs, nasal speech, swallowing difficulties with preserved bulbar reflexes, vertical nystagmus, bilateral internuclear ophthalmoparesis, and acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Compressive spinal cord lesion was excluded — “compressive cord lesion dismessed by tomographic study”  
2. Infectious etiologies were considered but ruled out by serology and cultures — “negative workup to more common infectious agents”  
3. Neuromyelitis optica was highly considered based on the prodrome, rapidly progressive transverse myelitis with brainstem signs, CSF inflammation, and exclusion of other causes — “the diagnosis of neuromyelitis optica (NMO) was highly considered”
